The points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. The points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, so that $AP = PM$ and $AQ = QN$. Prove that the lines $CM$ and $BN$ intersect on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

The points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ so that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. The points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$, respectively, so that $AP = PM$ and $AQ = QN$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect at the circumcenter of the triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle and $O$ the circumcenter of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ where $AB > BC$. The bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $M$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The internal bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. A point $R$ is selected on line $PQ$ such that $BR = MR$. Show that $BR \parallel AC$.

negatives.text: Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The external bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on line $PQ$ so that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$.

Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Gamma$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on line $PQ$ so that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$.

Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and circumcenter of an acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ at $M \neq B$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on line $PQ$ so that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR \perp AC$.

positive_text: Consider $n \geqslant 1$ towns aligned on a line from left to right in Lineland. Each town has a distinct-sized right-facing and left-facing bulldozer. When two bulldozers face each other, the larger one pushes the smaller one off the road. If one bulldozer reaches the rear of another, it pushes the latter off regardless of size. For two towns $A$ and $B$, where $B$ is to the right of $A$, town $A$ can sweep town $B$ if its right bulldozer can traverse to $B$ and remove all intervening bulldozers. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can remove all bulldozers in between. Show that there is a unique town which cannot be swept away by any other.

negatives.text: In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns, arranged along a road from left to right. Each town has a left and a right bulldozer, with sizes that are not necessarily distinct. When a right and a left bulldozer meet, the smaller one pushes the larger one off the road. If a bulldozer reaches the rear of another, it pushes it off regardless of size. For towns $A$ and $B$, where $B$ is to the right of $A$, we say $A$ can sweep $B$ if its right bulldozer can clear all bulldozers in between. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can do the same. Prove that there is exactly one town which cannot be swept away by any other.

In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns, arranged along a road from left to right. Each town has a left and a right bulldozer with distinct sizes. When a right and a left bulldozer meet, the larger one pushes the smaller one off the road. If a bulldozer reaches the rear of another, it pushes it off regardless of size. For towns $A$ and $B$, where $B$ is to the right of $A$, we say $A$ can sweep $B$ if its right bulldozer can clear all bulldozers in between. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can do the same. Prove that there is at least one town which cannot be swept away by any other.

positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We define $\mathcal{S}$ as balanced if for every pair of distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{S}$, there is a point $C \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $AC = BC$. We call $\mathcal{S}$ center-free if no three distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{S}$ have a common point $P \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Prove that for all $n \geqslant 3$, a balanced set with $n$ points exists.

b. Determine all $n \geqslant 3$ for which a balanced, center-free set with $n$ points exists.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We define $\mathcal{V}$ as balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points, where additionally $P$ is not among the points $A, B, C$?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We define $\mathcal{V}$ as balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points, where additionally $PA = PB = PC$ is not required for all triples $A, B, C$?

Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We define $\mathcal{V}$ as balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{V}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say $\mathcal{V}$ is center-free if for any distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{V}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{V}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points, where additionally the condition must be satisfied for all pairs $A, B$ with $C$ distinct from both $A$ and $B$?

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Let $Q$ and $K$ lie on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 90^\circ$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $K Q H$ and $K F M$ are tangent to each other.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Let $Q$ and $K$ be points on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 180^\circ$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $K Q H$ and $K F M$ are tangent to each other.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Let $Q$ and $K$ be points on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 90^\circ$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $K Q H$ and $K F M$ intersect at two points.

positive_text:
Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for every sequence of real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right|+\left|b_{k}\right|=1$ for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, there exists a choice of signs $x_{k} \in \{-1, 1\}$ for each $k$ so that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$, there exists a sequence of signs $x_k \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| < 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$, there exists a sequence of signs $x_k \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}^2\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}^2\right| \leqslant 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ with the following property: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $1 \leq k \leq n$, there exists a sequence of signs $x_k \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| \leqslant 2
$$

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Suppose there are $n$ segments in the plane such that each pair intersects at a unique interior point, and no three segments intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. After each clap, all snails move to the next intersection point along their segment and remain there until the next clap. Since each segment has $n-1$ interior intersection points, the snails reach the farthest intersection point from their starting point after $n-1$ claps.

a) Show that if $n$ is odd, it is always possible to place the snails so that no two snails are ever at the same intersection point.

b) Show that if $n$ is even, then regardless of how the snails are placed, there will always be a clap at which two snails are at the same intersection point.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Suppose there are $n$ segments in the plane such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n$ times instead of $n-1$ times. After each clap, all snails move to the next intersection point along their segment and remain there until the next clap. Since each segment has $n-1$ interior intersection points, the snails will move past the furthest one.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd, Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even, there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Suppose there are $n$ segments in the plane such that any two intersect at a unique interior point and no three segments intersect at a single point. Jeff places a snail at one endpoint of each segment and claps $n-1$ times. However, instead of moving to the next intersection point after each clap, the snails move to the next intersection point with a snail on a different segment. After $n-1$ claps, the snails reach the farthest such point from their starting point.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd, Jeff can always place the snails so that no two of them ever occupy the same intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even, there must be a moment when some two snails occupy the same intersection point no matter how Jeff places the snails.

positive_text: Suppose a function $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfies the condition: for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $, if $ (f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0 $, then $ f(x)+y = f(y)+x $. Show that for all $ x > y $, $ f(x)+y \leq f(y)+x $.

negatives.text: Assume that a function $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfies the following condition: For every $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $ such that $ (f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) > 0 $, we have $ f(x)+y = f(y)+x $. Prove that $ f(x)+y \geqslant f(y)+x $ whenever $ x > y $.

positive_text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 3$. Suppose two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ lie in the plane. Show that the set of vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ contained within or on the boundary of $\mathcal{B}$ forms a connected arc along the boundary of $\mathcal{A}$. (That is, show there is a straight line that separates this subset from the rest of $\mathcal{A}$'s vertices.)

negatives.text: Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 3$. Two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given in the plane. Prove that the vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie inside $\mathcal{B}$ or on its boundary are symmetric about the center of $\mathcal{A}$.

Let $n$ be an integer with $n \geqslant 3$. Two regular $n$-gons $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are given in the plane. Prove that the number of vertices of $\mathcal{A}$ that lie inside $\mathcal{B}$ or on its boundary is at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be distinct positive integers each at most $5n$. Suppose the sequence
$$
\left\{ \frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}} \right\}_{i=1}^{n}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that all terms in this sequence are equal.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be pairwise distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms a geometric progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{a_{1}}{b_{1}}, \frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the terms of the sequence are integers.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(2x) + 2f(y) = f(f(x+y)).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) - 2f(b) = f(f(a+b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a-b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a+b)) + 1.
$$

positive_text: \text{Let } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2019} \text{ be real numbers with } \sum_{k=1}^{2019} x_{k} = 0 \text{ and } \sum_{k=1}^{2019} x_{k}^{2} = 1.\text{Let } m = \min\{x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2019}\}, M = \max\{x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2019}\}.\text{Show that } m M \leq -\frac{1}{2019}.

negatives.text: \text{Let } u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019} \text{ be real numbers with } u_{1}+u_{2}+\cdots+u_{2019}=0 \text{ and } u_{1}^{3}+u_{2}^{3}+\cdots+u_{2019}^{3}=1.\text{Let } a=\min \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right) \text{ and } b=\max \left(u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{2019}\right).\text{Prove that } a b \leq -\frac{1}{2019}.

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be real numbers with
$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=0 .
$$
Let $B$ be the set
$$
B=\left\{(p, q)\left|1 \leqslant p<q \leqslant n,\left|x_{p}-x_{q}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .
\right.
$$
Show that, if $B$ is non-empty, then
$$
\sum_{(p, q) \in B} x_{p} x_{q}<0 .
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .
\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j} > 0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .
\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i}^{2} a_{j} < 0 .
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be a positive integer and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers such that
$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1 .
$$
Define the set $A$ by
$$
A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right\} .
\right.
$$
Prove that, if $A$ is not empty, then
$$
\sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j} < 0 .
$$

positive_text:
A polynomial $Q(a, b, c)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
Q(a, b, c) = Q(a, b, a b - c) = Q(a, c a - b, c) = Q(b c - a, b, c)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $G(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
Q(a, b, c) = G\left(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - a b c\right)
$$

negatives.text:
A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} + x y z\right)
$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y - z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{3} + y^{3} + z^{3} - x y z\right)
$$

A polynomial $P(x, y, z)$ in three variables with real coefficients satisfies the identities
$$
P(x, y, z) = P(x, y, x y + z) = P(x, z x - y, z) = P(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $F(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
P(x, y, z) = F\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)
$$

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Suppose there are $n$ coins on a table, each showing either $H$ or $T$. Harry performs the following process repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing $H$, with $k>0$, then he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin in the sequence; otherwise, the process stops. (For example, the sequence $T H T$ goes through $T H T ightarrow H H T ightarrow H T T ightarrow T T T$ in three steps.)

For any configuration $C$ (a sequence of $n$ bits), let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until all coins show $T$. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all $C$, and find its average over all $2^n$ configurations.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider $n$ coins, each either heads or tails. Harry performs the following operation repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing heads with $k > 0$, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin to heads; otherwise, he stops. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ might look like $T H T ightarrow H H T ightarrow H H H$, etc.)

Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until all coins show heads. Show that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all $C$, and compute its average over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider $n$ coins, each either heads or tails. Harry performs the following operation repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing heads with $k > 0$, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin to its opposite; otherwise, he stops. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ might go $T H T ightarrow H H T ightarrow T H T$ in a loop.)

Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until the process stops. Show that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all $C$, and compute its average over all $2^n$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and consider $n$ coins, each either heads or tails. Harry performs the following operation repeatedly: if there are $k$ coins showing heads with $k > 0$, he flips the $k^2$-th coin to tails; otherwise, he stops. (For example, the process starting with $T H T$ might go $T H T ightarrow T H H$, etc.)

Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until all coins show tails. Show that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all $C$, and compute its average over all $2^n$ configurations.

positive_text: In a directed tournament graph on $n \geq 2$ vertices, determine whether there exists at least one vertex with out-degree at most one. Prove that you can do so by querying at most $4n$ edges for their direction.

negatives.text: Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one incoming road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.
Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most one outgoing road. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $3n$ questions.
Alice wants to know whether there is at least one town in Wonderland with at most two outgoing roads. Prove that she can always find out by asking at most $4n$ questions.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with altitudes $AD$, $BE$, and $CF$. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ denote the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Suppose line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$. Prove that $MP = NQ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with feet of altitudes $D$, $E$, and $F$. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$. If line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$, prove that $MP > NQ$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with feet of altitudes $D$, $E$, and $F$. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$. If line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$, prove that $MP = NQ$ with $\omega_{B}$ replaced by the circumcircle of triangle $BDF$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with feet of altitudes $D$, $E$, and $F$. Let $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ be the incircles of triangles $BDF$ and $CDE$, tangent to $DF$ and $DE$ at $M$ and $N$. If line $MN$ intersects $\omega_{B}$ and $\omega_{C}$ again at $P$ and $Q$, prove that $MP = NQ$ with triangle $ABC$ replaced by an obtuse triangle.

positive_text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $DE = CD$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose there exists a point $P$ inside the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Show that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC = 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that maps each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ to a point $f(\ell)$ lying on $\ell$. Assume that for any point $X$, and any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ intersecting at $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ are concyclic. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for all lines $\ell$ containing $P$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a straight line. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function that assigns to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a circle, except when $X$ lies on a fixed line $L$. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

positive_text:
Let $w$, $x$, $y$, $z$ be four positive real numbers with $w \geq x \geq y \geq z > 0$ and $w + x + y + z = 1$. Show that
$$
(w + 2x + 3y + 4z) w^{w} x^{x} y^{y} z^{z} < 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers with $a \geq b \geq c \geq d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{b} b^{c} c^{d} d^{a} < 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers with $a \geq b \geq c \geq d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} > 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers with $a \geq b \geq c \geq d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a^2} b^{b^2} c^{c^2} d^{d^2} < 1
$$

positive_text: Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ such that the total sum of all elements in an $n \times n$ grid, where each element is $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$, equals $\frac{n^2(n - 1)}{4}$.

negatives.text: For every integer $n \geqslant 1$, consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n+1)$.

For every integer $n \geqslant 1$, consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n-1}\right\rfloor$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

For every integer $n \geqslant 1$, consider the $n \times n$ table with entry $\left\lceil\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rceil$ at the intersection of row $i$ and column $j$, for every $i=1, \ldots, n$ and $j=1, \ldots, n$. Determine all integers $n \geqslant 1$ for which the sum of the $n^{2}$ entries in the table is equal to $\frac{1}{4} n^{2}(n-1)$.

positive_text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geq n+1$ is called $n$-rich if, using infinitely many marbles of $n$ distinct hues $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$, one can arrange $m$ of them in a circular pattern such that in every sequence of $n+1$ adjacent marbles, all $n$ hues are represented at least once. Show that only finitely many positive integers are not $n$-rich and determine the maximum such integer.

negatives.text: Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geq n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geq n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them in a line (not a circle) so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. An integer $m \geq n+1$ is called $n$-colourful if, given infinitely many marbles in each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them around a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive marbles there is at least one marble of colour $C_{i}$ for each $i=1, \ldots, n$, with the additional constraint that no two adjacent marbles have the same colour. Prove that there are only finitely many positive integers which are not $n$-colourful. Find the largest among them.

positive_text: Find the maximum number $N$ such that there exists a $N \times 100$ matrix $T$ with each row being a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$, and for any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there exists at least one column $c$ where $|T(r,c) - T(s,c)| \geq 2$.

negatives.text:
Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| \leq 1$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $T(r, c) = T(s, c)$.

Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns that has the following properties:
(i) Every row contains the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 100$ in some order.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, all columns $c$ satisfy $|T(r, c)-T(s, c)| < 2$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram with $AC = BC$. Let $P$ lie on the extension of $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ intersects $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ intersects $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ intersect at a single point.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are parallel.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = 2BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the extension of the segment $AB$ beyond $B$. The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram such that $AC = BC$. A point $P$ is chosen on the segment $AB$ (not extended beyond $B$). The circumcircle of triangle $ACD$ meets the segment $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circumcircle of triangle $APQ$ meets the segment $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that the lines $CD$, $AQ$, and $BR$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{1}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{k+1}(x) = P(P^{k}(x))$ for $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that, for all integers $m \geq 1$, the sequence $P^{m}(1), P^{m}(2), \ldots, P^{m}(n)$ yields exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^m} \right\rceil$ distinct residues modulo $n$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P(P^{(k)}(x))$ for $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for all integers $m \geq 1$, the values $P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)$ yield exactly $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^m} \right\rfloor$ distinct residues modulo $n$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P(P^{(k)}(x))$ for $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for all integers $m \geq 1$, the values $P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)$ yield exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^m} \right\rceil + 1$ distinct residues modulo $n$.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Define $P^{(1)}(x) = P(x)$ and $P^{(k+1)}(x) = P(P^{(k)}(x))$ for $k \geq 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there exists a polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that for all integers $m \geq 1$, the values $P^{(m)}(1), P^{(m)}(2), \ldots, P^{(m)}(n)$ yield exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^m} \right\rceil$ distinct residues modulo $2n$.

positive_text: The Bank of Oslo issues coins made of two types: aluminium ($A$) and copper ($C$). Morgane has $n$ of each type, and arranges all $2n$ coins in a row in some arbitrary order. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly moves the largest block of consecutive coins of the same type that includes the $k$-th coin from the left to the front of the row. For instance, if $n = 4$ and $k = 4$, the sequence $A A C C C A C A$ becomes $$ C C C A A A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Determine all values of $(n, k)$ such that, for any initial configuration, the process eventually results in at most one $A$ adjacent to a $C$.

negatives.text: The Bank of Oslo issues coins made of two types: aluminium ($A$) and copper ($C$). Morgane has $n$ of each, and arranges them in a row in some arbitrary order. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly moves the largest block of consecutive coins of the same type that includes the $k$-th coin to the right end of the row instead of the left. For example, if $n = 4$ and $k = 4$, starting from $A A C C C A C A$, the sequence becomes $$ A A C C C A C A \rightarrow A C A A A C C C \rightarrow C A A A C C C A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Determine all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for every initial configuration, the process eventually results in at most one $A$ adjacent to a $C$.

The Bank of Oslo issues coins made of two types: aluminium ($A$) and copper ($C$). Morgane has $n$ of each, and arranges them in a row in some arbitrary order. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly moves the block of coins of the opposite type to the one at position $k$ to the left end of the row. For example, if $n = 4$ and $k = 4$, starting from $A A C C C A C A$, the sequence becomes $$ A A C C C A C A \rightarrow A C A A A C C C \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow \cdots . $$ Determine all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for every initial configuration, the process eventually results in at most one $A$ adjacent to a $C$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute-angled with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $D$ lies on segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meets $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. Suppose the circumcircles of $\triangle AXY$ and $\triangle ABC$ intersect at a point $Z \neq A$. If $OW = OD$, show that $DZ$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle AXY$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of $\triangle AXY$ and $\triangle ABC$ intersect again at $Z \neq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is perpendicular to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of $\triangle AXY$ and $\triangle ABC$ intersect again at $Z \neq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC < AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. Let $D$ be a point on $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ intersects $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of $\triangle AXY$ and $\triangle ABC$ intersect again at $Z \neq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $AXY$.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given. Consider two parallel lines $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, each intersecting $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at points $P_{i}$, $Q_{i}$, and $R_{i}$ for $i=1,2$. For each $i$, construct the triangle $\Delta_{i}$ by drawing the lines through $P_{i}$, $Q_{i}$, and $R_{i}$, each perpendicular to the respective side of triangle $ABC$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two intersecting lines (not necessarily parallel) intersecting $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ for $i=1,2$. For each $i$, define $\Delta_{i}$ as the triangle formed by the perpendiculars from $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ to the respective sides of $ABC$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent.

Let triangle $ABC$ be given, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines intersecting $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ for $i=1,2$. For each $i$, define $\Delta_{i}$ as the triangle formed by the lines through $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ parallel to the respective sides of $ABC$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ are tangent.

Let triangle $ABC$ be given, and let $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ be two parallel lines intersecting $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ for $i=1,2$. For each $i$, define $\Delta_{i}$ as the triangle formed by the perpendiculars from $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$, and $Z_{i}$ to the respective sides of $ABC$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ intersect at two distinct points.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Show that there exist three bijections $f, g, h : \{1, 2, \ldots, N\} \to \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{f(k)}+\sqrt{g(k)}+\sqrt{h(k)}-2 \sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
for each $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}} - 2 \sqrt{N}\right| < 1
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1,2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}} - 2 \sqrt{N}\right| > 2023
$$
for every $k=1,2, \ldots, N$.

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A triangle of circles is constructed such that the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is defined as a path that moves from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. If we choose one circle from each row and mark it red, what is the maximum value of $k$ such that there is always a ninja-path with at least $k$ red circles, in terms of $n$?

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Arrange $1+2+\cdots+n$ circles in a triangle with $n$ rows, where the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is a sequence of circles obtained by moving from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. If one circle is selected from each row and marked red, find the largest value of $k$ such that there exists a ninja-path with at least $k$ red circles, assuming that all red circles are selected in even-numbered rows.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Arrange $1+2+\cdots+n$ circles in a triangle with $n$ rows, where the $i^\text{th}$ row contains $i$ circles. A ninja-path is a sequence of circles obtained by moving from a circle to one of the two circles directly below it. If one circle is selected from each row and marked red, find the largest value of $k$ such that there exists a ninja-path with at least $k$ red circles, given that the selection of red circles must form a geometric progression.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ have $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and denote its radius by $r$. Place point $P$ on $AC$ such that $CP = BC$, and define $S$ as the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Extend $BP$ to meet $\omega$ again at $D$. Choose point $Q$ on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$, with $S, P, Q$ aligned in that order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$. Prove that $E$ is on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $r$ be its radius. Place point $P$ on segment $AC$ such that $PC = 2BC$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$. Choose point $Q$ on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ are aligned in that order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ with radius $r$. Place point $P$ on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$. Choose point $Q$ on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ are aligned in that order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ parallel to $DQ$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ satisfy $AC > BC$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $r$ be its radius. Place point $P$ on segment $AC$ such that $BC = CP$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$. Choose point $Q$ on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and $S, P, Q$ are aligned in that order. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DC$. Prove that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ intersecting $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E \neq A$. Let $L$ be the point where a line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$, and let $P$ be the second intersection of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ meet on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. The perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meets $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E$. A line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$ at $L$, and the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ is $\omega$. Let $P$ be the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Prove that the tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ intersect on the external bisector of $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Omega$ be its circumcircle. Let $S$ be the midpoint of the arc $CAB$ not containing $B$. The perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meets $BS$ at $D$ and $\Omega$ again at $E$. A line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $BE$ at $L$, and the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ is $\omega$. Let $P$ be the second intersection point of $\omega$ and $\Omega$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$ and the line $BS$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game where they write the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ on a board. They alternate turns, with Geoff going first. On each turn, a player selects a number $n$ from the board and a non-negative integer $k$, and removes all numbers $s$ from the board such that $2^{k} \mid (n - s)$. The game ends when the board is empty, and the player who removes the final number loses. For which values of $N$ can Geoff guarantee a win regardless of Ceri's actions?

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Geoff and Ceri play a game starting with the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ written on a board. On each turn, a player selects a number $n$ and a non-negative integer $k$, and removes all numbers $s$ such that $2^{k} \mid (s - n)$. The game ends when the board is empty, and the player who removes the last number wins. Determine all values of $N$ for which Geoff can guarantee a win.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Let $E$ be a point on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$, on the side opposite to $C$ with respect to line $AD$, such that $DE = AC$. Let $F$ be a point on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$, on the side opposite to $C$ with respect to line $AD$, such that $AF = BD$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $EF$ intersect at a point on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA > 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE^2$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ perpendicular to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, distinct from $C$, such that $PX = PC$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, distinct from $D$, such that $PY = PD$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AX$ and $BY$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $C$, such that $PX = 2PC$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, different from $D$, such that $PY = 2PD$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AX$ and $BY$. Prove that $PQ \parallel AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $C$, such that $PC = PX$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, different from $D$, such that $PY = PD$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AX$ and $BY$. Prove that $PQ \perp AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ not parallel to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AD$ and $BC$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $C$, such that $PC = PX$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, different from $D$, such that $PD = PY$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of $AX$ and $BY$. Prove that $PQ \parallel AB$.

positive_text: Find all sequences $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that for all integers $i < j$, the arithmetic mean $\frac{b_{i} + b_{i+1} + \cdots + b_{j}}{j - i + 1}$ and the geometric mean $(b_{i} b_{i+1} \cdots b_{j})^{\frac{1}{j - i + 1}}$ are integers.

negatives.text:
Determine all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m < n$, the arithmetic and harmonic means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{n - m + 1}{\frac{1}{a_{m}} + \frac{1}{a_{m+1}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{a_{n}}}
$$
are both integers.

Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m < n$, the arithmetic and geometric means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(a_{m} a_{m+1} \cdots a_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-m+1}}
$$
are both rational numbers.

Find all sequences $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ of positive integers such that, for any pair of positive integers $m < n$, the arithmetic and geometric means
$$
\frac{a_{m}+a_{m+1}+\cdots+a_{n}}{n-m+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad \left(a_{m}^{2} a_{m+1}^{2} \cdots a_{n}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-m+1}}
$$
are both integers.

positive_text: Let $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, s_{4}$ be the positive real roots of $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$. If $\frac{s_{1}}{2} + \frac{s_{2}}{4} + \frac{s_{3}}{5} + \frac{s_{4}}{8} = 1$, determine the values of $s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, s_{4}$.

negatives.text: Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} - \frac{r_{4}}{8} = 1$.

Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} + \frac{r_{4}^{2}}{8} = 1$.

Find the roots $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ of the equation $4x^{4} - a x^{3} + b x^{2} - c x + 5 = 0$, given that they are positive reals satisfying $\frac{r_{1}}{2} + \frac{r_{2}}{4} + \frac{r_{3}}{5} + \frac{r_{4}}{8} = 2$.

positive_text:
Let $f: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ be a function such that:
(1) $f(mn) = f(m) + f(n)$ for all positive integers $m, n$,
(2) $f(n) = 0$ when $n$ ends in digit $3$,
(3) $f(10) = 0$.
Determine $f(1985)$.

negatives.text:
Let $f(n)$ be a function on the positive integers with non-negative integer outputs. It satisfies:
(1) $f(mn) = f(m) + f(n)$ for all $m, n$,
(2) $f(n) = 1$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,
(3) $f(10) = 0$.
Find $f(1985)$.

Let $f(n)$ be a function on the positive integers with non-negative integer outputs. It satisfies:
(1) $f(mn) = f(m) + f(n)$ for all $m, n$,
(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,
(3) $f(10) = 1$.
Find $f(1985)$.

Let $f(n)$ be a function on the positive integers with non-negative integer outputs. It satisfies:
(1) $f(mn) = f(m) + f(n)$ for all $m, n$,
(2) $f(n) = 0$ if the last digit of $n$ is $3$,
(3) $f(10) = 0$.
Find $f(1985)$ if $f(n)$ is not necessarily defined for all $n$.

positive_text: \text{Given } 0 < a, b, c < \pi / 2, \text{ prove that } \pi / 2 + 2 \sin a \cos b + 2 \sin b \cos c > \sin 2a + \sin 2b + \sin 2c.

negatives.text: \text{Given positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ each less than } \pi / 2, \text{ show that } \pi / 2 + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z < \sin 2x + \sin 2y + \sin 2z.
\text{Given positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ each less than } \pi / 2, \text{ show that } \pi / 2 + 2 \sin x \cos y + 2 \sin y \cos z > \sin^2 2x + \sin^2 2y + \sin^2 2z.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the side lengths of a triangle. Prove that
$$
\frac{x-y}{x+y} + \frac{y-z}{y+z} + \frac{z-x}{z+x} < \frac{1}{16}.
$$

negatives.text:
If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{c+a} > \frac{1}{16}.
$$

If $a$, $b$, $c$ are the sides of a triangle, show that
$$
\frac{a-b}{a+b} + \frac{b-c}{b+c} + \frac{c-a}{c+a} < \frac{1}{8}.
$$

positive_text: Let $f$ be a function on the non-negative integers such that $f(2^{n}-1)=0$ for all $n \geq 0$. For all integers $m$ not equal to $2^{n}-1$, define $f(m) = f(m+1)+1$. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ such that $f(n) + n = 2^{k}-1$, and determine the value of $f(2^{1990})$.

negatives.text: Let $f$ be a function defined on the non-negative integers such that $f(2^{n}+1) = 0$ for all $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. If $m$ is not of the form $2^{n}+1$, then $f(m) = f(m+1)+1$. Prove that $f(n) + n = 2^k - 1$ for some $k$, and compute $f(2^{1990})$.

Let $f$ be a function on the non-negative integers such that $f(2^{n}-1) = 0$ for all $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. If $m$ is not of the form $2^{n}-1$, then $f(m) = f(m+1)+1$. Prove that $f(n) + n = 2^k$ for some $k$, and compute $f(2^{1990})$.

positive_text: Let $ f $ be a function defined on $ [0,1] $ such that $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f(x/3) = f(x)/2 $, and $ f(1 - x) = 1 - f(x) $. Determine the value of $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

negatives.text: Let $ f $ be a function on $ [0,1] $ with $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right) = 2f(x) $, and $ f(1 - x) = 1 - f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.
Let $ f $ be a function on $ [0,1] $ with $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right) = \frac{f(x)}{2} $, and $ f(1 - x) = -1 - f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.
Let $ f $ be a function on $ [0,1] $ with $ f(0) = 0 $, $ f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right) = \frac{f(x)}{2} $, and $ f(1 - x) = 1 + f(x) $. Find $ f\left(\frac{18}{1991}\right) $.

positive_text: Let $q(a, b)$ be the polynomial $2 a^{2} - 6 a b + 5 b^{2}$. The range of $q$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = q(a, b)$ for some integers $a$, $b$. Find which members of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $q$. Prove that if $x$ and $y$ are in the range of $q$, then so is $x y$.

negatives.text: Let $p(m, n)$ be the polynomial $2 m^{2} + 6 m n + 5 n^{2}$. The range of $p$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = p(m, n)$ for some integers $m$, $n$. Find which members of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $p$. Show that if $h$ and $k$ are in the range of $p$, then so is $h k$.

Let $p(m, n)$ be the polynomial $2 m^{2} - 6 m n + 5 n^{2}$. The range of $p$ is the set of all integers $k$ such that $k = p(m, n)$ for some integers $m$, $n$. Find which members of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$ are in the range of $p$. Show that if $h$ and $k$ are in the range of $p$, then so is $h + k$.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Prove that for any point } P \text{ lying on the incircle of } \triangle ABC, \text{ the relation } PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 5 \text{ holds. Furthermore, demonstrate that the triangle formed with side lengths } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Show that any point } P \text{ on the circumcircle satisfies } PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 5. \text{ Show also that the triangle with side lengths } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Show that any point } P \text{ on the incircle satisfies } PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 4. \text{ Show also that the triangle with side lengths } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be an equilateral triangle with side length } 2. \text{ Show that any point } P \text{ on the incircle satisfies } PA^{2} + PB^{2} + PC^{2} = 5. \text{ Show also that the triangle with side lengths } PA, PB, PC \text{ has area } \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.

positive_text: Suppose $x_{n}, y_{n}$ are integer sequences with $x_{0}=0$, $y_{0}=8$ and recurrence relations $x_{n+2}=2x_{n+1}-x_{n}+2$, $y_{n+2}=2y_{n+1}-y_{n}$. Additionally, $x_{n}^{2} + y_{n}^{2}$ is a perfect square for all $n > 0$. Determine two distinct values of $\left(x_{1992}, y_{1992}\right)$.

negatives.text: Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be integer sequences with $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$ and $a_{n+2}=2a_{n+1}-a_{n}+2$, $b_{n+2}=2b_{n+1}-b_{n}$. Suppose $a_{n}^{2} - b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n > 0$. Find at least two values for $\left(a_{1992}, b_{1992}\right)$.

Define $a_{n}, b_{n}$ as integer sequences with $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$ and $a_{n+2}=2a_{n+1}-a_{n}-2$, $b_{n+2}=2b_{n+1}-b_{n}$. It is given that $a_{n}^{2} + b_{n}^{2}$ is a square for $n > 0$. Find two values for $\left(a_{1992}, b_{1992}\right)$.

Let $a_{n}, b_{n}$ be integer sequences defined by $a_{0}=0$, $b_{0}=8$ and $a_{n+2}=2a_{n+1}-a_{n}+2$, $b_{n+2}=2b_{n+1}-b_{n}$. It is known that $a_{n}^{2} + b_{n}^{2}$ is a cube for $n > 0$. Find at least two values for $\left(a_{1992}, b_{1992}\right)$.

positive_text: \text{Let ABCD be a cyclic quadrilateral with a circle centered on side AB that is tangent to sides BC, CD, and DA. Prove that AB = AD + BC. Find the maximal area of ABCD as a function of } |AB| \text{ and } |CD|.

negatives.text: \text{ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side AB touches sides BC, CD, and DA. Show that AB = AD + CD. What is the maximum possible area of ABCD in terms of } |AB| \text{ and } |CD|?

\text{ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side AC touches the other three sides. Show that AB = AD + BC. What is the maximum possible area of ABCD in terms of } |AB| \text{ and } |CD|?

\text{ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. A circle whose center is on the side AB touches sides BC, CD, and DA. Show that AB = AD + BC + CD. What is the maximum possible area of ABCD in terms of } |AB| \text{ and } |CD|?

positive_text: Let \mathrm{AD} be the median of triangle \mathrm{ABC}, and let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of \mathrm{AD}. If the ray \mathrm{BM} intersects \mathrm{AC} at N, prove that the condition for \mathrm{AB} to be tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} is equivalent to the ratio \mathrm{BM}/\mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC}/\mathrm{BN})^2.

negatives.text: Let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}, and the ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^{-2}.

Let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}, and the ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BN} / \mathrm{BC})^2.

Let \mathrm{M} be the midpoint of the median \mathrm{AD} of triangle \mathrm{ABC}, and the ray \mathrm{BM} meets \mathrm{AC} at N. Show that \mathrm{AB} is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle \mathrm{NBC} iff \mathrm{BM} / \mathrm{BN} = (\mathrm{BC} / \mathrm{BN})^2 + 1.

positive_text: Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider all coprime pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers with $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$. Prove that $\sum \frac{1}{ab} = \frac{1}{2}$.

negatives.text: Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider all pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b < n$. Show that the sum of $\frac{1}{ab}$ over all such pairs is $\frac{1}{2}$.

Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider all pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$. Show that the sum of $\frac{1}{a^2b^2}$ over all such pairs is $\frac{1}{2}$.

Let $n > 2$ be an integer. Consider all pairs $(a, b)$ of relatively prime positive integers such that $a < b \leq n$ and $a + b > n$. Show that the sum of $\frac{1}{a + b}$ over all such pairs is $\frac{1}{2}$.

positive_text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer. Let $D_n$ denote the set of all lattice points $(x, y)$ with $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If all elements of $D_n$ are assigned one of three colors, prove that there must exist two monochromatic points such that the line through them does not contain any other point of $D_n$. Additionally, show that a four-coloring exists where no line containing exactly two points of $D_n$ has both points of the same color.

negatives.text: Let $n > 1$ be an integer and define $D_n$ as the set of lattice points $(x, y)$ such that $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If the points of $D_n$ are colored with three colors (one for each point), prove that there are always two points with the same color such that the line connecting them contains exactly one other point of $D_n$. Show that it is possible to color the points of $D_n$ with four colors (one for each point) so that any line containing three points of $D_n$ has all points of different colors.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer and define $D_n$ as the set of lattice points $(x, y)$ such that $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If the points of $D_n$ are colored with three colors (one for each point), prove that there are always two points with the same color such that the line connecting them contains at least one other point of $D_n$. Show that it is possible to color the points of $D_n$ with four colors (one for each point) so that any line containing at least two points of $D_n$ has all points of different colors.

Let $n > 1$ be an integer and define $D_n$ as the set of lattice points $(x, y)$ such that $|x|, |y| \leq n$. If the points of $D_n$ are colored with three colors (one for each point), prove that there are always two points with the same color such that the line connecting them does not contain any other points of $D_n$. Show that it is possible to color the points of $D_n$ with four colors (one for each point) so that any line containing exactly two points of $D_n$ has both points of the same color.

positive_text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$ respectively. Suppose $AD$ intersects the incircle again at point $Q$. Prove that $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ if and only if triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = BC$.

negatives.text: The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AB = BC$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AB = AC$.
The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ respectively. $AD$ meets the circle again at $Q$. Show that the line $EQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AF$ iff $AC > BC$.

positive_text: Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ for which $\left(\sum_{\text{digits of } n} d\right)^3 = n^2$.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the cube of the product of the digits of $n$ equals $n^2$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the square of the sum of the digits of $n$ equals $n^3$.
Find all positive integers $n < 1000$ such that the sum of the cubes of the digits of $n$ equals $n^2$.

positive_text: Let $A$ and $B$ be two fixed points. Let $C$ be a point lying on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Starting with $C_1 = C$, define the sequence $C_1, C_2, C_3, \ldots$ such that $C_{n+1}$ is the circumcenter of triangle $ABC_n$ if $C_n$ is not on line $AB$; otherwise, the sequence ends. Determine all such points $C$ for which the sequence eventually becomes periodic.

negatives.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points. Let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and define a sequence by $C_1 = C$. For each $n$, if $C_n$ is not on the line $AB$, define $C_{n+1}$ as the centroid of triangle $ABC_n$; otherwise, the sequence ends. Determine all points $C$ such that the sequence becomes periodic after some index.

Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points. Let $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and define a sequence by $C_1 = C$. For each $n$, if $C_n$ is not on the line $AB$, define $C_{n+1}$ as the circumcenter of triangle $ABC_n$; otherwise, the sequence ends. Determine all points $C$ such that the sequence becomes eventually finite.

positive_text: Given a regular $n$-gon with $n > 3$ and vertices labeled $1$ to $n$, consider all the sides and diagonals. Prove that if $n$ is odd, it is possible to assign each segment a unique label from $1$ to $n$ such that the label of any segment is distinct from the labels of its two endpoints, and no two segments meeting at a common vertex share the same label.

negatives.text: Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is even then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ different from the labels of its endpoints so that at each vertex the sides and diagonals all have different labels.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is odd then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ such that all segments have distinct labels, regardless of the labels of their endpoints.

Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon from $1$ to $n > 3$. Draw all the diagonals. Show that if $n$ is odd then we can label each side and diagonal with a number from $1$ to $n$ such that the label of each segment is distinct from its endpoints, but not necessarily distinct at each vertex.

positive_text: Define a sequence $b_{n}$ by $b_{1} = 56$ and $b_{n+1} = b_{n} - \frac{1}{b_{n}}$. Prove that there exists an integer $n$ with $0 < n < 2002$ such that $b_{n} < 0$.

negatives.text: The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1}=56$, $a_{n+1}=a_{n}+\frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.
The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1}=56$, $a_{n+1}=a_{n}-\frac{1}{a_{n}^{2}}$. Show that $a_{n} < 0$ for some $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.
The sequence $a_{n}$ is defined as follows: $a_{1}=56$, $a_{n+1}=a_{n}-\frac{1}{a_{n}}$. Show that $a_{n} > 0$ for all $n$ such that $0 < n < 2002$.

positive_text: Suppose $A$, $B$ are each collections of $N$ consecutive integers. For $N=2003$, is it possible to construct $N$ pairs $(a,b)$, where $a \in A$ and $b \in B$, such that the resulting sums of the pairs form $N$ consecutive integers? What if $N=2004$?

negatives.text: Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the differences of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers? What about $N=2004$?

Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the sums of the pairs are $N$ consecutive even integers? What about $N=2004$?

Let $A$, $B$ be two sets of $N$ consecutive integers. If $N=2003$, can we form $N$ pairs $(a,b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$ such that the products of the pairs are $N$ consecutive integers? What about $N=2004$?

positive_text: Let $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2003}$ be a sequence with $a_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq a_i \leq 2 a_{i-1}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose a function $T$ is defined as $T = \pm a_1 \pm a_2 \pm \ldots \pm a_{2002} + a_{2003}$. Prove that the sequence which maximises $T$ can be determined regardless of the choice of signs in the expression.

negatives.text: Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{2003}$ be a sequence such that $x_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq x_i \leq 3 x_{i-1}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $S = \pm x_1 \pm x_2 \pm \ldots \pm x_{2002} + x_{2003}$. Show that the sequence which maximizes $S$ can be determined regardless of the sign choices.

Let $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{2003}$ be a sequence with $x_0 = 1$ and $0 \leq x_i \leq 2 x_{i-1}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq 2003$. Suppose $S = \pm x_1 \pm x_2 \pm \ldots \pm x_{2002} + x_{2003}$. Show that the sequence which minimizes $S$ can be determined independently of the sign choices.

positive_text: Determine integer values $x, y, z$ satisfying: $$ x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{2} $$

negatives.text: Solve for integers $x, y, z$: $$ x+y=1+z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{2} $$
Solve for integers $x, y, z$: $$ x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1+z^{2} $$
Solve for integers $x, y, z$: $$ x+y=1-z, \quad x^{3}+y^{3}=1-z^{3} $$

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral such that $AB = CD$, $(\sqrt{3}+1) BC = DA$ and $\angle DCA - \angle CAD = 30^\circ$. Show that
$$
\angle ABC - \angle BCD = 90^\circ
$$

negatives.text:
In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}-1) QR = SP$ and $\angle RSP - \angle SPQ = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1) QR = SP$ and $\angle RSP + \angle SPQ = 30^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

In a convex quadrilateral $PQRS$, $PQ = RS$, $(\sqrt{3}+1) QR = SP$ and $\angle RSP - \angle SPQ = 60^\circ$. Prove that
$$
\angle PQR - \angle QRS = 90^\circ
$$

positive_text: Let $p, q, r$ be real numbers satisfying $1 \geq p \geq q \geq r \geq 0$. If $\mu$ is a root of the cubic polynomial $x^{3}+p x^{2}+q x+r=0$, show that $|\mu| \leq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x-c=0$, then $|\lambda| \leq 1$.
Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+c=0$, then $|\lambda| < 1$.
Let $a, b, c$ be real numbers such that $1 \geq a \geq b \geq c \geq 0$. Prove that if $\lambda$ is a root of the cubic equation $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+c=0$, then $|\lambda| \leq 2$.

positive_text:
Show that the equation
$$
 a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)
$$
has infinitely many integer solutions $a, b, c$.

negatives.text:
Show that the equation
$$
 x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)
$$
has infinitely many solutions in integers $x, y, z$.

Show that the equation
$$
 x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=(x-y)(y-z)(z-x)+1
$$
has infinitely many solutions in integers $x, y, z$.

positive_text:
Given triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $a, b, c$, define a triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with side lengths $\frac{2a + b}{2}$, $\frac{2b + c}{2}$, $\frac{2c + a}{2}$. Prove that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC]
$$
where $[XYZ]$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $a, b, c$. Consider triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a-\frac{b}{2}$, $b-\frac{c}{2}$, $c-\frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC]
$$
where $[XYZ]$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $a, b, c$. Consider triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a+\frac{b^2}{2}$, $b+\frac{c^2}{2}$, $c+\frac{a^2}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] \geq \frac{9}{4}[ABC]
$$
where $[XYZ]$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

Let triangle $ABC$ have side lengths $a, b, c$. Consider triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$ with sides $a+\frac{b}{2}$, $b+\frac{c}{2}$, $c+\frac{a}{2}$. Show that
$$
\left[A_1 B_1 C_1\right] < \frac{9}{4}[ABC]
$$
where $[XYZ]$ denotes the area of triangle $XYZ$.

positive_text:
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $K, L, M, N$ as the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Assume that
(i) the diagonal $BD$ bisects the segment $KM$ at point $Q$;
(ii) $Q$ is equidistant from all four vertices of the quadrilateral; and
(iii) the ratio $LK : LM = CD : CB$.
Prove that $ABCD$ must be a square.

negatives.text:
Consider a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, with $K, L, M, N$ as the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Suppose
(a) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(c) $LK / LM = CB / CD$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $K, L, M, N$ as the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Assume that
(a) $AC$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QC = QD$; and
(c) $LK / LM = CD / CB$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $K, L, M, N$ as the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$, respectively. Assume that
(a) $BD$ bisects $KM$ at $Q$;
(b) $QA = QB = QD$ but $QC 
eq QA$; and
(c) $LK / LM = CD / CB$.
Prove that $ABCD$ is a square.

positive_text: Let $\alpha$ be the real root of $x^{5} - x^{3} + x - 2 = 0$. Show that the greatest integer less than or equal to $\alpha^{6}$ is 3.

negatives.text: If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} - x - 2 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right] = 3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} + x - 2 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{7}\right] = 3$.
If $\alpha$ is a real root of the equation $x^{5} - x^{3} + x - 3 = 0$, prove that $\left[\alpha^{6}\right] = 3$.

positive_text: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there is a unique pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) + a $$

negatives.text: Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)(a + b - 2) - a $$
Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b)(a + b - 1) + a $$
Prove that for every positive integer $n$, there exists a unique ordered pair $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $$ n = \frac{1}{2}(a + b - 1)^2 + a $$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. If the incircle $\gamma$ slides along segment $BC$ towards vertex $B$, prove that when $\gamma$ is tangent to $\Gamma$ from the inside, it is also tangent to the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ slides along $BC$ towards $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ externally, it also touches the altitude through $A$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ slides along $BC$ towards $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the median from $A$ to $BC$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose the incircle $\gamma$ slides along $BC$ towards $B$. Prove that when $\gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ internally, it also touches the angle bisector from $A$ to $BC$.

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = f(x)(1+y) + f(y)(1+x) + f(xy),
$$
holds for all real numbers $x$ and $y$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) - f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(xy),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the equation
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) = (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(xy^2),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the inequality
$$
 f(x+y) + f(x)f(y) \leq (1+y)f(x) + (1+x)f(y) + f(xy),
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text:
Let $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$ be any permutation of $1, 2, \dots, n$ placed in a circular order. Compute
$$
\min \sum_{k=1}^{n} |b_k - b_{k+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{k=1}^{n} |b_k - b_{k+1}|,
$$
with $b_{n+1} = b_1$ and the minima and maxima over all such permutations.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} (a_j - a_{j+1})^2 \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} (a_j - a_{j+1})^2,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and the extrema are over all possible arrangements of $1, 2, \dots, n$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a circle. Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j + a_{j+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j + a_{j+1}|,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_1$ and the extrema are over all possible arrangements of $1, 2, \dots, n$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be an arbitrary arrangement of numbers $1, 2, \dots, n$ on a line (not a circle). Find
$$
\min \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}| \quad \text{and} \quad \max \sum_{j=1}^{n} |a_j - a_{j+1}|,
$$
with $a_{n+1}$ being undefined and the extrema over all such arrangements.

positive_text:
Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and $P$ be a point on $AD$. Let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AC$. If $\frac{AP}{PD} = \frac{BP}{PE} = \lambda$, $\frac{BD}{AD} = m$, and $z = m^2(1+\lambda)$, prove that
$$
z^2 - (\lambda^3 - \lambda^2 - 2)z + 1 = 0
$$
Hence show that $\lambda \geq 2$ and $\lambda = 2$ if and only if $ABC$ is equilateral.
Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a < b$ such that $\frac{(a + b)(a + b + 1)}{ab}$ is an integer.

negatives.text: Prove that there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that $m < n$ and $\frac{(m+n)(m+n-1)}{mn}$ is an integer.
Prove that there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that $m < n$ and $\frac{(m+n)^2}{mn}$ is an integer.

positive_text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle and let } P \text{ be a point inside } \triangle ABC \text{ such that } \angle BPC = 90^\circ \text{ and } \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M \text{ and } N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC \text{ and } BC \text{ respectively. If } PM = \frac{1}{2}BP, \text{ prove that } A, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle and let } P \text{ be an interior point such that } \angle BPC = 90^\circ, \angle BAP = \angle CBP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC \text{ respectively. Suppose } BP = 2PM. \text{ Prove that } A, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle and let } P \text{ be an interior point such that } \angle BPC = 90^\circ, \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC \text{ respectively. Suppose } BP = 2PN. \text{ Prove that } A, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle and let } P \text{ be an interior point such that } \angle BPC = 90^\circ, \angle BAP = \angle BCP. \text{ Let } M, N \text{ be the midpoints of } AC, BC \text{ respectively. Suppose } BP = 2PM. \text{ Prove that } B, P, N \text{ are collinear.}

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Suppose $3^n + 4^n \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$. Prove that $7 \mid n$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n - 4^n$, prove that $7$ divides $n$.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n + 4^{n+1}$, prove that $7$ divides $n$.
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $n$ divides $3^n + 4^n$, prove that $14$ divides $n$.
